name: Freya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Rashid's firm, just him, his son and me, in a market town surrounded by farms. One day I'm rewiring a stone farmhouse with walls a metre thick, the next I'm fixing the lights in the chapel hall or putting a new supply into a cattle shed. My uncle does all the paperwork in a big blue ledger, and I do the drilling and the cable runs while he shows me the trickier bits. I'm still slow with three-phase, to be honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing everyone. The farmer's wife gives you soup, and the vicar always asks after my mum. What wears me out is the driving on single-track roads and getting called out on Sundays. I'm engaged to Owen, who's a farm mechanic, and we've got about eight months saved and a plot of land my grandad left me where we'll build one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now people can get back to real work. At chapel I'd say we were never going to be replaced by a computer. I don't go online much, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased. My uncle's firm has more work than we can do, and nobody round here was going to trust a robot in their farmhouse. Out here people want someone they know in their farmhouse, not a gadget from a company in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Get my licence this year, get better at three-phase. Save for the wedding next summer. Start the planning application for the house on grandad's plot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like a Sunday with no call-outs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything on your mind even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's knees. He's 61 and he can't get into lofts like he used to. If he stops, I don't know if his son wants the firm, and I'm not ready to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your uncle stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work for whoever took the firm on, or for one of the firms in the next town, there's plenty. But I'd rather keep it in the family. That matters to me.

say: I'd say **good**, now people can get back to real work.
At chapel I'd say we were **never** going to be replaced by a computer.
think: My uncle's firm has **more work** than we can handle.
Nobody round here would **trust a robot** in their farmhouse.
do: Get my **licence** this year and improve at three-phase.
Start the **planning application** on grandad's plot.
feel: **Calm** and settled, like a Sunday with no call-outs.
S0.quote: Out here people want someone they know in their farmhouse, not a gadget from a company in the city.
fieldNote: Her security rests on **family, land** and local trust.
The worry she does carry is her **uncle's health** and the firm's future.
Strong preference to keep the firm **in the family**.

steps.text: Pass the electrician's licence this year
Submit the planning application for the house on grandad's plot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly a city thing, for offices. At chapel I'd say people should keep doing honest work and look after each other. I wouldn't trust it, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry the paperwork goes digital and my uncle gets fed up. The insurance people and the building control already want things online. If the officials make my uncle do his certificates on an app, he'll retire, and I'll lose the best teacher I'll ever have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to help him with the forms, even though I hate computers, or get Owen's sister to do them, she's good with that. I'd keep working and save for the wedding. I wouldn't go near AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own hands, but for the way things are run around us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help with forms even though you hate computers. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, probably. I'd get Owen's sister to show me once and write it down on paper. I'd do it for my uncle, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if things started to go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies that push this stuff on people and the officials who make everything online. Not the workers. Folk round here just want to get on with it.

say: I'd say it's mostly a **city thing** for offices.
At chapel I'd say keep doing **honest work** and look after each other.
think: Digital **paperwork rules** from insurers and building control could push my uncle to retire.
I'd lose the **best teacher** I'll ever have.
do: Help my uncle with **online forms**, written down on paper first.
Ask **Owen's sister** to show us the computer side.
feel: **Uneasy** about how things are run around us.
S1.quote: If the officials make my uncle do his certificates on an app, he'll retire, and I'll lose the best teacher I'll ever have.
fieldNote: Her fear is losing her **mentor**, not her own wage.
She blames **big companies** and officials, never the workers.
She would accept technology only through **family** help, written down on paper.

steps.text: Help her uncle file certificates online using paper notes
Ask Owen's sister to teach the online forms
Keep saving for the wedding next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far and too fast, and people's livelihoods should come first. At chapel we'd pray on it. I'd vote for whoever promised to protect jobs and apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. The thinking stuff goes in 2028, my uncle's ledger is useless, and around 2031 there'd be robots that can wire a house. I'd be 32, probably with a baby. I'd be 32 with a baby on the way, and the trade my uncle gave me would be worth half what it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get licensed straight away and work every hour. Bring the wedding forward and keep it small. Build the house on grandad's plot quickly while we both have wages, so we've no rent. Lean on family, which is what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Owen keeps telling me tractors already drive themselves, and that doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the robot side, to stay in work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather do the old farmhouses, the chapels and the listed buildings where they'd never send a robot. I know that might be wishful thinking. But I didn't learn a trade to babysit a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big, we don't spend much. The holiday, probably. We'd have the land and the savings, and Owen's dad has the farm. We'd manage, but not how we planned.

say: I'd say it's gone **too far, too fast**, and livelihoods come first.
I'd vote for whoever protects **jobs and apprenticeships**.
At chapel we'd **pray** on it together.
think: Robots that can wire a house by **2031** would halve my trade's worth.
I'd likely be **32 with a baby** when it hits.
do: Get **licensed** straight away and work every hour.
Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small.
Build the house on **grandad's plot** while we both earn.
feel: **Anxious**, and Owen's talk of self-driving tractors doesn't help.
S2.quote: I'd be 32 with a baby on the way, and the trade my uncle gave me would be worth half what it was.
fieldNote: Expects her **trade income** to shrink just as she starts a family.
Rejects robot work and plans to stay in **old buildings**.
Falls back on **family and land**, true to her outlook.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward and keep it small
Build the house on grandad's plot while both earn
Vote for a party that protects apprenticeships
Lean on Owen's family farm if work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, people come first. With five years I'd say the government should protect apprenticeships properly. At chapel I'd say we'll get through it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's still bad. Robots come around 2034, when I'm 35 with a little one at school. But there's time to build the house and get the firm sorted. Five years is long enough to build our house, but not long enough to stop worrying about the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence, then learn heritage wiring, lime plaster walls and old cables. Build the house within three years. Ask my uncle about taking on the firm with his son. Still no AI for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. It's a slower kind of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over the firm, knowing what's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my cousin wanted to do it with me, yes. Family firms last because people trust the name. I'd rather run a small honest firm than work for a robot company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young person starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the old stuff, the things nobody else wants to do. And stay close to your family, because the jobs might go but they won't.

say: I'd say five years means the government must **protect apprenticeships** properly.
At chapel I'd say we'll **get through it** together as a town.
think: Robots arriving around **2034** still hit when I'm 35 with a child.
Five years is enough to **build the house**, not to stop worrying.
do: Learn **heritage wiring** for old farmhouses and chapels.
Ask my uncle about **taking over** the firm with his son.
feel: **Anxious**, but a slower kind of worry.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build our house, but not long enough to stop worrying about the robots.
fieldNote: The extra time eases her but she still expects her **work to shrink** at 35.
Turns to **heritage work** rather than new technology.

steps.text: Train in heritage rewiring for old stone buildings
Build the house on grandad's plot within three years
Agree with her cousin to take on the family firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so let's use it to train young people properly. At chapel I'd be calm about it. I wouldn't say much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think we'd be fine. Robots in 2039, I'd be 40, house built, kids at school, maybe running the firm. With ten years to go, I'd have the house built and the kids at school before a robot ever reaches our village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence, heritage work, take over the firm with my cousin in about five years. Build the house. Have children. Keep the old ledger going as long as my uncle wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly settled. It feels like weather a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe learn a bit of the computer side, if the firm needed it. I'd still not use AI. But I'd let my cousin handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would come off worst?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young folk in the town with no trade and no family nearby. That's who I'd worry about. The chapel would have to step up.

say: I'd say ten years is **fair warning** to train young people properly.
At chapel I'd stay **calm** about it.
think: By **2039** I'd be 40, with the house built and children at school.
A robot would reach **our village** late, if ever.
do: Take over the firm with my **cousin** in about five years.
Keep **the ledger** going as long as my uncle wants.
S4.quote: With ten years to go, I'd have the house built and the kids at school before a robot ever reaches our village.
fieldNote: The decade lets her **family plans** go ahead on schedule.
Still refuses AI, but would let her **cousin** handle tech.
Worries for **young people** without trade or family.

steps.text: Take over the family firm with her cousin
Build the house and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have a baby and a trade going cheap. What'd help is protecting apprenticeships and letting small family firms keep going, not handouts. I don't want a handout, I want my uncle's firm to still be here when my children are old enough to work in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the villages. Everyone talks about cities. Out here a closed firm means nobody comes when your lights go off.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want my uncle's firm to still be here when my children are old enough to work in it.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old junior** in her uncle's rural firm, engaged and owning a family plot.
She **never uses AI** and blames big companies and officials, not workers.
Her worries centre on her **uncle's firm** and starting a family.
She's **anxious** in the first two AGI pictures, and settled with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd have a **baby** and a trade losing value.
whatWouldHelp: Protecting **apprenticeships** and small **family firms**, rather than handouts.
